facts.claim: The division of nutrients into total fat versus carbohydrate appears to be less helpful in predicting outcomes.
facts.quote: The division of nutrients into total fat (regardless of fatty acids) versus carbohydrate (type and quantity not specified) appears to be less helpful in predicting outcomes.

facts.claim: Diets higher in monounsaturated fatty acids, fiber, and low glycemic index foods appear to have advantages in insulin resistance, glycemic control and blood lipids in a number of studies.
facts.quote: Diets that are higher in monounsaturated fatty acids, fiber and low glycemic index foods appear to have advantages in insulin resistance, glycemic control and blood lipids in a number of studies.

facts.claim: The current evidence strongly supports a diet with reduced content of fat and sugar-rich beverages, and more carbohydrates rich in fibre and grain (whole grain foods, fruit and vegetables) and protein (lean meat and dairy products) as the best choice for the prevention of weight gain, obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
facts.quote: The current evidence strongly supports a diet with reduced content of fat and sugar-rich beverages, and more carbohydrates rich in fibre and grain (whole grain foods, fruit and vegetables) and protein (lean meat and dairy products) as the best choice for the prevention of weight gain, obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

facts.claim: The evidence linking particular fatty acids to body fatness is weak.
facts.quote: The evidence linking particular fatty acids to body fatness is weak.

facts.claim: All hypocaloric regimens are suitable, as long as they work, for any given subject.
facts.quote: All hypocaloric regimens are suitable, as long as they work, for any given subject.

research.angle: While the proposed angle suggests low-fat products cause weight gain via carbohydrate substitution, the evidence actually supports a low-fat diet combined with high-fiber carbohydrates and protein as a primary choice for preventing obesity.
research.verdict: The sources do not provide evidence that low-fat dairy products specifically cause weight gain; instead, they suggest that a low-fat diet with high fiber and protein is a supported strategy for weight management.
research.caveat: The research highlights that the 'best diet' for weight loss is not yet identified and may need to be prescribed on an individual basis.
